$comment: Bestiary demons: malware families and groups. Sources include MITRE ATT&CK (© The MITRE Corporation; reproduced and distributed with permission). status: active | exorcised (law-enforcement takedown, see exorcism) | dormant.
attackTerms: MITRE ATT&CK Terms of Use grant 'a non-exclusive, royalty-free license to use ATT&CK for research, development, and commercial purposes'; 'Any copy you make for such purposes is authorized provided that you reproduce MITRE's copyright designation and this license in any such copy.' Verdict: reuse on a public non-commercial site is allowed (non-commercial use is a fortiori covered) provided the site reproduces the copyright notice ('© <year> The MITRE Corporation. This work is reproduced and distributed with the permission of The MITRE Corporation.') and the license text, and respects MITRE trademark rules (ATT&CK® is a registered trademark; no implied endorsement). Source: https://attack.mitre.org/resources/legal-and-branding/terms-of-use/ (fetched 2026-10-24).

demons.name: Morris Worm
defenses: Remove debug/backdoor features from network daemons
Avoid trust-based remote login (rsh/rexec); require authentication
Enforce strong passwords
demons.summary: Released by Robert Tappan Morris in November 1988, it spread across Unix hosts via a sendmail debug mode, a fingerd buffer overflow and weak passwords/rsh trust. A re-infection bug made it overload thousands of machines, an estimated tenth of the early Internet. It led to the first US conviction under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and to the creation of CERT/CC.

demons.name: ILOVEYOU
defenses: Do not open unexpected attachments; show file extensions
Block script attachments (.vbs, .js) at the mail gateway
Disable Windows Script Host where unneeded
demons.summary: A VBScript mass-mailing worm released from the Philippines on 4 May 2000, spreading as 'LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT.vbs' through Outlook address books. It overwrote local files and infected tens of millions of Windows PCs within days. Its author could not be prosecuted because the Philippines lacked a cybercrime law at the time.

demons.name: Code Red
defenses: Patch internet-facing web servers promptly (MS01-033)
Remove unused ISAPI extensions/handlers
Filter and monitor anomalous outbound traffic
demons.summary: A memory-resident worm that exploited a buffer overflow in the IIS Indexing Service (idq.dll) in July 2001. It defaced pages with 'Hacked By Chinese!' and launched a DDoS against the White House website, infecting over 350,000 hosts in under 14 hours. The variant Code Red II installed a backdoor.

demons.name: SQL Slammer
defenses: Patch database servers (MS02-039) and keep them off the internet
Block UDP 1434 at the perimeter
Apply egress filtering
demons.summary: A 376-byte worm that hit on 25 January 2003, exploiting a buffer overflow in the Microsoft SQL Server Resolution Service over a single UDP packet. It infected about 75,000 hosts in roughly ten minutes, the fastest-spreading worm then recorded, slowing large parts of the Internet and disrupting ATMs and emergency services. The patch had been available for six months.

demons.name: Blaster
defenses: Patch promptly (MS03-026)
Enable host firewall and block RPC/DCOM (TCP 135) from untrusted networks
demons.summary: A worm that spread in August 2003 by exploiting a buffer overflow in the Windows DCOM RPC interface, causing repeated reboots on infected machines. It carried a message to Bill Gates and was programmed to flood windowsupdate.com. It pushed Microsoft toward enabling the Windows Firewall by default in XP SP2.

demons.name: Sasser
defenses: Patch promptly (MS04-011)
Block SMB/LSASS ports (TCP 445, 139) from untrusted networks
Enable host firewall
demons.summary: A self-propagating worm released in April-May 2004 that exploited a buffer overflow in the Windows LSASS service, requiring no user interaction. It crashed and rebooted machines worldwide, disrupting airlines, hospitals and news agencies. Its author, a German teenager, also wrote Netsky variants and was convicted in 2005.

demons.name: Mydoom
relatedEvents: 2009 DDoS on US and South Korean sites
defenses: Filter executable and archive attachments at the mail gateway
User awareness on unexpected attachments
Keep antivirus signatures current
demons.summary: A mass-mailing worm first seen on 26 January 2004 that became the fastest-spreading email worm on record, at one point carried by a large share of all email. It opened a backdoor and launched DDoS attacks against SCO Group. Its author was never identified, and variants were reused in 2009 DDoS attacks on US and South Korean websites.

demons.name: Conficker
relatedEvents: Infections at UK Ministry of Defence and French Navy
defenses: Patch MS08-067 and keep legacy systems updated
Disable AutoRun/AutoPlay for removable media
Enforce strong admin passwords and account lockout
demons.summary: A worm first detected in November 2008 that exploited the Windows Server service flaw MS08-067, spread via USB drives and weak network-share passwords, and used domain-generation algorithms for command and control. It built a botnet of millions of PCs, prompting the industry Conficker Working Group to pre-register its domains. It never delivered a major payload but lingered on unpatched systems for over a decade.

demons.name: Mirai
defenses: Change default credentials on IoT devices
Disable Telnet/remote admin on internet-facing devices
Segment and firmware-update IoT devices
demons.summary: IoT botnet malware that scans for devices such as cameras and routers using factory-default Telnet credentials and enlists them for DDoS attacks. In 2016 it produced record attacks, including the Dyn DNS outage that disrupted major websites. Its source code was published in September 2016 and its three authors pleaded guilty in the US in December 2017; countless variants remain active.

demons.name: Emotet

exorcism.by: Europol/Eurojust with NL, DE, US, UK, FR, LT, CA, UA
exorcism.note: Botnet resurfaced Nov 2021; low activity since 2023

relatedEvents: Malspam campaigns delivering TrickBot and Ryuk
defenses: Block macros in Office documents from the internet
Filter malspam attachments and links at the mail gateway
Segment networks and limit admin share access to slow lateral movement
demons.summary: Emotet began in 2014 as a banking trojan and evolved into a malware-loading botnet sold as access to other criminals, spread mostly by malicious Office documents. Europol called it the world's most dangerous malware when an international operation took over its infrastructure on 27 January 2021 and pushed an uninstall update. It re-emerged in November 2021 with TrickBot's help but has been largely quiet since 2023.

demons.name: GameOver Zeus

exorcism.by: FBI/DOJ with Europol, NCA and private partners

relatedEvents: Theft of over $100 million from bank accounts
defenses: Use out-of-band transaction verification for online banking
Keep endpoints patched and run EDR
Block known C2 and DGA domains
demons.summary: A peer-to-peer variant of the ZeuS banking trojan operated by Evgeniy Bogachev's group, used to steal online banking credentials and to distribute CryptoLocker ransomware. Its decentralised design made it resilient to takedown. The US-led Operation Tovar disrupted both GameOver Zeus and CryptoLocker in June 2014, and Bogachev remains on the FBI's most-wanted list.

demons.name: Qakbot

exorcism.by: FBI/DOJ with FR, DE, NL, UK, RO, LV
exorcism.note: Date is the DOJ announcement; takedown action ran in the preceding days

relatedEvents: Initial access for Conti, Black Basta, REvil and ProLock ransomware
defenses: Block macro and HTML/OneNote/ISO attachments from email
Monitor for email thread hijacking and suspicious child processes of Office
Enforce MFA and least-privilege to blunt lateral movement
demons.summary: Qakbot started around 2007-2008 as a banking trojan and became a major malware loader, often hijacking email reply chains to spread and selling access to ransomware gangs. In the FBI-led Operation Duck Hunt in late August 2023, agents redirected infected computers to FBI servers and issued an uninstaller to over 700,000 machines. Smaller campaigns reappeared afterwards and its alleged leader was indicted in May 2025.

demons.name: TrickBot

exorcism.note: Operators shifted to other tools by 2022

relatedEvents: Ryuk and Conti attacks on US hospitals (2020)
defenses: Patch MS17-010 and disable SMBv1
Block malspam attachments and monitor for Emotet/BazarLoader droppers
Protect credentials (LSASS protection, MFA) and segment networks
demons.summary: A modular banking trojan that emerged in 2016 from the Dyre lineage and became a botnet and ransomware delivery platform run by the Wizard Spider group, behind Ryuk and Conti. Microsoft led a court-ordered infrastructure disruption in October 2020, and the operators shifted to other tools by 2022.

demons.name: Necurs
defenses: Filter spam and malicious attachments at the gateway
Block known DGA domains
Keep endpoints patched and monitored
demons.summary: One of the largest spam botnets, active from about 2012, which infected over nine million computers and distributed Dridex, Locky ransomware and fraud spam. Microsoft obtained a US court order in March 2020 to seize its infrastructure and pre-empt its domain generation algorithm. It has been largely inactive since.

demons.name: CryptoLocker

exorcism.by: FBI/DOJ with Europol, NCA and private partners

defenses: Keep offline, tested backups
Block executable attachments in email
Restrict write access to network shares
demons.summary: Ransomware first seen in September 2013 that encrypted files with RSA keys and demanded payment in Bitcoin, setting the template for modern ransomware. It was distributed largely through the GameOver Zeus botnet and reportedly extorted millions of dollars. Operation Tovar disrupted it in June 2014, after which a decryption service was released.

demons.name: WannaCry
defenses: Patch MS17-010 and disable SMBv1
Block TCP 445 from the internet
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: A ransomware worm released on 12 May 2017 that spread automatically via EternalBlue, the exploit attributed to the NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers, infecting over 200,000 computers in 150 countries including NHS hospitals. Spread was halted when a researcher registered its kill-switch domain. The US and UK attributed it to North Korea's Lazarus Group.

demons.name: Ryuk
relatedEvents: Attacks on US hospitals during COVID-19
defenses: Remove TrickBot/Emotet/BazarLoader footholds quickly
Protect domain admin credentials and patch Zerologon
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: Big-game-hunting ransomware first seen in August 2018, operated by Wizard Spider and typically deployed after TrickBot or BazarLoader infections. It targeted hospitals, municipalities and newspapers and demanded large ransoms. It faded in 2021 as the operators moved to Conti.

demons.name: REvil

exorcism.by: Europol/Eurojust with 17 countries; DOJ charges vs Kaseya attacker

defenses: Patch and restrict internet-exposed management software (RMM, WebLogic)
Enforce MFA on remote access
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: A ransomware-as-a-service operation run by GOLD SOUTHFIELD that emerged in 2019 as the likely successor of GandCrab and embraced double extortion at scale. Its July 2021 attack via Kaseya VSA hit up to 1,500 businesses. Affiliates were arrested in Romania and elsewhere in Europol's Operation GoldDust in November 2021, and Russia's FSB detained members in January 2022.

demons.name: Conti
defenses: Patch internet-facing systems (Log4j, ProxyShell, Zerologon)
Detect Cobalt Strike and remove TrickBot/BazarLoader footholds
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: A ransomware-as-a-service operation linked to Wizard Spider, first seen in late 2019 and one of the most prolific gangs of 2020-2022. It crippled Ireland's health service in 2021 and led Costa Rica to declare a national emergency in 2022. After internal chats leaked in early 2022 it shut down in May-June 2022, with members dispersing to other groups.

demons.name: LockBit

exorcism.by: UK NCA, FBI, Europol and partners

defenses: Patch edge devices quickly (Citrix, Fortinet, PaperCut)
Enforce MFA on RDP/VPN and restrict RDP exposure
Keep offline backups and test restores
demons.summary: A ransomware-as-a-service operation first seen in 2019 that became the most deployed ransomware worldwide in 2022-2023. In Operation Cronos the UK NCA, FBI and international partners took control of its infrastructure on 19-20 February 2024, recovered decryption keys and later named its alleged administrator. The group attempted relaunches afterwards but with far lower impact.

demons.name: Cl0p
defenses: Patch and isolate managed file transfer servers
Restrict internet exposure of file-transfer and ERP systems
Monitor for webshells and large outbound transfers
demons.summary: Ransomware linked to the financially motivated TA505/FIN11 cluster, first seen in 2019. Since 2020 the group has specialised in mass exploitation of zero-days in file-transfer products, stealing data from hundreds of organisations at once and extorting them, as in the 2023 MOVEit campaign. It remains active.

demons.name: BlackCat
relatedEvents: MGM Resorts attack (2023, with Scattered Spider)
defenses: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA and harden help-desk identity verification
Monitor for remote access tools and ESXi encryption
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: Ransomware-as-a-service first seen in November 2021, notable as the first major ransomware written in Rust and able to target Windows, Linux and VMware ESXi. The FBI disrupted it in December 2023 and released a decryptor to over 500 victims. After the 2024 Change Healthcare attack its operators staged an apparent exit scam and went dark.

demons.name: DarkSide
defenses: Enforce MFA on VPNs and disable unused accounts
Separate IT from OT networks
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: A ransomware-as-a-service operation first seen in August 2020. Its May 2021 attack on Colonial Pipeline caused fuel shortages on the US East Coast; the DOJ later recovered 63.7 of the 75 bitcoin paid (about $2.3 million). DarkSide announced it was shutting down days later and is widely seen as having rebranded as BlackMatter.

demons.name: Hive

exorcism.by: FBI/DOJ with DE, NL and Europol

relatedEvents: Costa Rica public health service attack (2022)
defenses: Patch Exchange (ProxyShell) and FortiOS
Enforce MFA on remote access
Keep offline backups
demons.summary: Ransomware-as-a-service first seen in June 2021 that targeted hospitals, schools, financial firms and critical infrastructure, extorting over 1,500 victims. The FBI infiltrated its network in July 2022, passed decryption keys to victims, and with German and Dutch partners seized its servers in January 2023. It is believed to have rebranded as Hunters International.

demons.name: Maze
defenses: Patch VPN appliances (Pulse Secure)
Restrict RDP exposure and enforce MFA
Monitor large outbound data transfers
demons.summary: Ransomware first seen in May 2019 that popularised double extortion, publishing stolen data when victims refused to pay. It operated as a 'cartel' with other gangs. Its operators announced retirement in November 2020, with affiliates moving to Egregor.

demons.name: Shamoon
defenses: Keep offline backups and rebuild plans for workstations
Protect and monitor privileged credentials
Segment networks to limit wiper propagation
demons.summary: A destructive wiper used in August 2012 against Saudi Aramco, where it rendered around 30,000 workstations unusable and displayed a burning-flag image. New versions struck Gulf targets in 2016-2017 and Italy's Saipem in 2018. The attacks are associated with Iranian state-linked actors.

demons.name: NotPetya
defenses: Patch MS17-010 and disable SMBv1
Vet and monitor software update channels (supply chain)
Limit admin credentials reuse and keep offline backups
demons.summary: A wiper disguised as ransomware launched on 27 June 2017 through a trojanised update of the Ukrainian accounting software M.E.Doc. It spread with EternalBlue, EternalRomance and stolen credentials, causing an estimated $10 billion in damage worldwide. The US, UK and others attributed it to Russia's GRU Sandworm unit, whose officers were indicted in 2020.

demons.name: Olympic Destroyer
relatedEvents: PyeongChang 2018 Winter Olympics opening ceremony disruption
defenses: Protect credentials (LSASS protection, unique admin passwords)
Keep offline backups and incident playbooks for events
Segment event networks
demons.summary: A wiper that disrupted IT systems during the opening ceremony of the PyeongChang Winter Olympics on 9 February 2018. It contained deliberate false flags pointing to other countries' hackers. The US DOJ indicted Russian GRU (Sandworm) officers for the attack in 2020.

demons.name: WhisperGate
defenses: Keep offline backups
Enforce MFA and patch internet-facing systems
Monitor for MBR overwrites and mass file corruption
demons.summary: A wiper disguised as ransomware that hit Ukrainian government and IT organisations in mid-January 2022, ahead of Russia's full-scale invasion. It overwrote the master boot record and corrupted files with no real recovery option. The US charged a Russian national and GRU officers in connection with it in 2024.

demons.name: HermeticWiper
defenses: Keep offline backups
Monitor abuse of legitimate signed drivers
Restrict Group Policy and domain admin rights
demons.summary: A wiper deployed against Ukrainian organisations on 23 February 2022, the eve of Russia's invasion. It abused a legitimately signed EaseUS partition driver to corrupt disks and was sometimes paired with a decoy ransomware and a worm component. Microsoft linked it with moderate confidence to IRIDIUM (Sandworm), which the US attributes to GRU Unit 74455; some vendors and press linked it to Sandworm, while ESET found no tangible link to a known actor.

demons.name: AcidRain
relatedEvents: Viasat KA-SAT satellite modem outage (24 February 2022)
defenses: Harden and segment management networks of service providers
Secure VPN access (patching, MFA)
Monitor firmware/update pushes to customer devices
demons.summary: A wiper for MIPS-based modems and routers used on 24 February 2022 against Viasat's KA-SAT network, bricking tens of thousands of satellite modems across Europe. The outage also cut remote monitoring of thousands of German wind turbines. The EU, US and UK attributed the attack to Russia.

demons.name: Stuxnet
defenses: Air-gap discipline and control of removable media
Whitelist applications and monitor PLC logic changes
Patch engineering workstations
demons.summary: A sophisticated worm discovered in June 2010 that targeted Siemens Step7 software and PLCs controlling Iranian uranium-enrichment centrifuges, subtly altering their speed while hiding its changes. It spread via USB drives using several Windows zero-days and stolen code-signing certificates. It is widely reported as a joint US-Israeli operation and was the first known cyberweapon to cause physical destruction.

demons.name: Flame
relatedEvents: Espionage in Iran and the Middle East (discovered 2012)
defenses: Monitor for unusual Windows Update/proxy activity
Retire MD5-based certificates
Control removable media
demons.summary: A large modular espionage toolkit publicly discovered in May 2012, mainly in Iran and the Middle East, able to record audio, screenshots, keystrokes and Bluetooth data. It spread through fake Windows Update using a forged Microsoft certificate created with an MD5 collision attack. Its operators sent a self-destruct command shortly after its exposure.

demons.name: Duqu
defenses: Patch font-parsing and kernel vulnerabilities
Block malicious Word attachments
Hunt for memory-resident implants
demons.summary: An espionage toolkit discovered in September 2011 that shared much code with Stuxnet and collected information useful for attacking industrial control systems. It was delivered via a Word document exploiting a TrueType font zero-day in the Windows kernel. A memory-only successor, Duqu 2.0, was found inside Kaspersky Lab and at venues of the Iran nuclear negotiations in 2015.

demons.name: Regin
defenses: Monitor telecom management networks (GSM base station controllers)
Hunt for stealthy kernel drivers and encrypted virtual file systems
Segment and monitor admin access
demons.summary: A highly stealthy, multi-stage espionage platform publicly exposed in November 2014 but active since at least 2008. It targeted telecom operators, governments and researchers, including Belgacom, and could monitor GSM networks. Reporting links it to the Five Eyes intelligence agencies.

demons.name: Pegasus
defenses: Keep iOS/Android updated promptly
Enable Lockdown Mode for high-risk users
Reboot devices regularly and use forensic checks (e.g. MVT)
demons.summary: Commercial spyware sold by Israel's NSO Group to governments, capable of fully compromising iPhones and Android phones, often through zero-click exploits. Investigations by Citizen Lab and Amnesty documented its use against journalists, activists and politicians. A US federal court found NSO liable for hacking WhatsApp users in December 2024; a jury set damages in May 2025.

demons.name: Industroyer
relatedEvents: Attempted attack on Ukrainian grid (April 2022, Industroyer2)
defenses: Segment OT networks and monitor IEC 104/61850 traffic
Restrict engineering access with MFA
Prepare manual operation fallbacks
demons.summary: Malware purpose-built to attack electrical substations by speaking industrial protocols such as IEC 101, IEC 104, IEC 61850 and OPC DA directly. It caused a power outage in part of Kyiv in December 2016. A variant, Industroyer2, was used in a foiled attack on a Ukrainian energy company in April 2022; both are attributed to Sandworm.

demons.name: Triton
relatedEvents: Attack on a Saudi petrochemical plant's safety systems (2017)
defenses: Keep safety controllers in program mode only when needed (physical key switch)
Isolate safety instrumented systems from IT
Monitor engineering workstations
demons.summary: Malware discovered in 2017 that targeted Schneider Electric Triconex safety instrumented systems at a Saudi petrochemical facility, the first known malware designed to disable industrial safety controls. It was discovered when a flaw triggered a plant shutdown. It is attributed to TEMP.Veles, linked to a Russian state research institute (TsNIIKhM) sanctioned by the US.

demons.name: Snake
relatedEvents: Espionage against NATO governments and journalists (≈20 years)
defenses: Hunt for kernel-level implants and covert P2P traffic
Apply vendor/CISA detection guidance
Restrict and monitor privileged access
demons.summary: A sophisticated cyber-espionage implant used for about two decades by Turla, a unit of Russia's FSB, to steal documents from hundreds of systems in at least 50 countries. Infected machines formed a covert peer-to-peer network. The FBI's Operation MEDUSA used a tool called PERSEUS to make the implants disable themselves in May 2023.

demons.name: Sandworm Team
defenses: Patch edge and mail servers quickly (e.g. Exim)
Segment and monitor OT networks
Keep offline backups against wipers
demons.summary: A destructive threat group attributed to Russia's GRU Unit 74455, active since at least 2009. It is responsible for the first blackouts caused by cyberattacks in Ukraine, NotPetya and Olympic Destroyer. Six of its officers were indicted by the US in 2020.

demons.name: Lazarus Group
defenses: Verify job offers and software from unsolicited contacts
Harden SWIFT and crypto signing infrastructure with multi-party approval
Patch internet-facing services
demons.summary: A North Korean state-sponsored group active since at least 2009 that combines espionage, destruction and large-scale financial theft. It is blamed for the Sony Pictures hack, the $81 million Bangladesh Bank heist, WannaCry and billions in cryptocurrency theft. The US has charged several North Korean operatives in connection with its activity.

demons.name: Zeus
relatedEvents: Theft from small business bank accounts (2009-2010)
defenses: Use out-of-band confirmation for banking transactions
Keep browsers and OS patched
Block known C2 domains and monitor web injects
demons.summary: A banking trojan kit first identified in 2007 that stole credentials through form grabbing and web injects, sold to many criminal crews. Its source code leaked in 2011; descendants include GameOver Zeus (built by Bogachev's group), Citadel and Zeus Panda, Citadel and Zeus Panda. The 2010 Operation Trident Breach led to arrests of money-mule networks in the US, UK and Ukraine.

demons.name: Dridex
relatedEvents: Bank credential theft of over $100 million
defenses: Block Office macros and RTF/OLE exploits
Filter malspam
Use transaction verification and monitor for credential theft
demons.summary: A banking trojan derived from Cridex/Bugat, active since 2014 and spread mainly by Office macro malspam via Necurs. It was operated by Evil Corp, whose leader Maksim Yakubets was charged and sanctioned by the US in December 2019. A 2015 law-enforcement disruption had limited effect; the group later moved into ransomware.

demons.name: Carbanak

exorcism.operation: Arrest of Carbanak/Cobalt leader in Spain
exorcism.by: Spanish National Police with Europol and FBI

relatedEvents: Theft of up to $1 billion from banks (2013-2018)
defenses: Block spearphishing attachments and patch Office
Monitor bank internal systems (ATM, SWIFT) for remote control tools
Segment payment networks
demons.summary: Backdoor malware used from about 2013 by a criminal group to infiltrate bank networks, record employees' screens, and cash out via ATMs and fraudulent transfers, with losses estimated up to a billion euros. Kaspersky exposed the campaign in 2015. The suspected leader was arrested in Spain in March 2018 in a Europol-coordinated operation.

demons.name: RedLine Stealer

exorcism.by: Dutch National Police with FBI, Eurojust and partners

relatedEvents: Mass credential theft feeding account takeovers and ransomware access
defenses: Avoid pirated software and malvertised downloads
Do not store passwords in browsers; use a password manager and MFA
Revoke session tokens after infection
demons.summary: An infostealer sold as malware-as-a-service since 2020 that harvests browser passwords, cookies, crypto wallets and system data. It was one of the most widespread stealers, spread via phishing, malvertising and fake software. Operation Magnus, led by Dutch police with the FBI, took over its servers in October 2024 and the US charged alleged developer Maxim Rudometov.

demons.name: Lumma Stealer

exorcism.by: Microsoft DCU, DOJ, Europol EC3, JC3

defenses: Train users against 'paste this command' fake CAPTCHA lures
Use a password manager and phishing-resistant MFA
Revoke sessions and rotate credentials after infection
demons.summary: An infostealer sold as malware-as-a-service since 2022 that steals browser credentials, cookies and crypto wallets, often delivered through fake CAPTCHA 'ClickFix' lures. Microsoft, the DOJ, Europol and Japan's JC3 disrupted it on 21 May 2025, seizing around 2,300 domains and its control panel. Researchers reported partial rebuilding of its infrastructure afterwards.

demons.name: Raccoon Stealer

exorcism.by: FBI with NL and IT authorities
exorcism.note: Charges announced 2022-10-25; Raccoon v2 emerged mid-2022

defenses: Avoid cracked software and malicious ads
Use password manager and MFA
Rotate credentials after infection
demons.summary: An infostealer sold as malware-as-a-service from 2019, stealing passwords, cookies and crypto wallets from millions of victims. In March 2022 the FBI and Dutch and Italian authorities dismantled its infrastructure, and Ukrainian national Mark Sokolovsky was arrested; the DOJ announced charges in October 2022. A version 2 appeared later in 2022.
